source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3, given the canonical two-step task as a text story, showed the model-based stay-probability signature.
numbers: 200 simulations, 20 repetitions of two stages each, 70/30 transitions. Stay probability fell after reward through a rare transition, t(1982) = -6.16, p < .001. Stay rose after a rare and unrewarded trial, t(1814) = 2.33, p = .01.
quote: GPT-3 relies on a deliberate model-based approach to solve the two-step task.
limits: Text-only history in the prompt, so the model can reason over the whole history. Same paper: GPT-3 picks the intuitive wrong answer on the CRT, so 'deliberate' depends on the task. Stay-probability signatures can be faked by model-free shortcuts (Akam et al. 2015).
agent_relevance: An LLM that sees the full transition history in context can act model-based without any learning. So the S0 gate should not assume the model is a pure habit machine.

source: Coda-Forno, Binz, Akata, Botvinick, Wang, Schulz (2024) CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab
finding: CogBench scores 'model-basedness' with the two-step task (regression interaction of reward x common transition) across many LLMs. Proprietary models that solve the task were at least human-level; GPT-4 was significantly above humans. Bigger models were more model-based.
numbers: Parameter count raised model-basedness (beta = 0.481, z = 4.2, p < 0.001). Training-set size and code training data had no significant effect. Relative gains in model-basedness: chain-of-thought +64.59 percent, step-back prompting +118.59 percent.
limits: The metric is an interaction beta, not a planning measure. Reward is equal for model-based and model-free agents by design, so performance does not show strategy. Prompts are text histories.
agent_relevance: Prompts that make the model abstract the problem (step-back) raised planning-like behaviour more than step-by-step CoT. Supports an S0 step that restates the task structure before choosing.

source: CogBench (2024): prompting effects and human-likeness
finding: No model matched humans on most of the ten behavioural metrics. High task performance does not mean human-like behaviour. CoT helps probabilistic reasoning more; step-back helps model-basedness more.
numbers: Probabilistic reasoning (posterior accuracy): CoT +9.01 percent, step-back +3.10 percent. Model-basedness: CoT +64.59, step-back +118.59 percent. RLHF made behaviour more human-like.
limits: Percentages are relative changes in normalised scores, so large percentages can be small absolute shifts.
agent_relevance: Choose the scaffold by what is missing: CoT for inference, abstraction for structure use.

source: Demircan, Saanum, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) Sparse autoencoders reveal temporal difference learning in large language models
finding: Llama 3 70B learns a simplified two-step-like MDP in context. Its choices fit a Q-learning (TD, value-caching) account better than a myopic one. A single TD-error feature found with a sparse autoencoder is causally needed.
numbers: 100 runs x 30 episodes, first 7 random. Q-learning NLL 2729 vs myopic 2864. Best SAE feature correlates with TD error r = 0.58 (block 34). Switching it off lowers return. Llama 8B stayed at chance.
limits: Deterministic transitions, not the stochastic 70/30 Daw task, so it cannot separate model-based from model-free. Only the 70B model learns.
agent_relevance: Inside an LLM, in-context learning can run on cached value-like signals, not only explicit lookahead. Capacity matters: small models cannot do it.

source: Demircan et al. (2024): graph learning and successor representation
finding: On graph learning, Llama's SAE latents correlate with the successor representation and its TD signals, and do better than model-based alternatives.
numbers: Figure 5: next-state prediction accuracy rises quickly, bottleneck states decodable from middle blocks, SR-like codes. Exact correlations not extracted.
limits: Based on the figure legend and text; numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Links to the sibling subfield on the successor representation, the planned-versus-cached compromise.

source: Paglieri, Cupial, et al. (2026) Learning When to Plan: Efficiently Allocating Test-Time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: Closest LLM analogue of arbitration between planning and acting. Always planning (ReAct-style) and never planning are both worse than planning at an intermediate frequency (a 'Goldilocks' zone). Prompting 'plan only when necessary' did not work zero-shot; SFT then RL did.
numbers: Crafter and POGS, 100 seeds, Llama-3.3-70B zero-shot curves. RL-trained 8B agent reward 0.387 vs 70B zero-shot 0.379 with 85 percent fewer output tokens. Plan completion 20 vs 16 percent, adaptive replanning 41 vs 35 percent. Goldilocks seen also with Gemini 2.5 Flash and TextWorld.
quote: Models struggled to consistently interpret abstract instructions such as 'plan only when necessary'
limits: Needs training. Framework has a token cost term C_tokens and an instability term C_noise. Environments are games. Zero-shot self-gating was unreliable.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S0: plan only when expected gain exceeds cost plus instability. Also a warning that a prompt rule alone collapses to always or never; give the gate an explicit signal.

source: Paglieri et al. (2026): cost penalty and steering
finding: A token-cost penalty regulates planning frequency in proportion to its size. Higher penalties cut explicit planning without badly hurting performance. Human-written plans let the trained agent finish Crafter (diamond), which no agent did alone.
numbers: Penalty swept in Appendix C.3. Autonomous agents never fully solved Crafter.
limits: Planning may be internalised in the weights, which hides it. Explicit plans kept for control.
agent_relevance: Pricing deliberation in tokens works as a knob, like Keramati's reward-rate cost. Keep plans explicit so they can be audited and overridden.

source: Paglieri et al. (2026): overthinking and instability
finding: The authors tie the loss from always planning to an instability cost: the always-plan agent backtracks most, and long contexts may dilute attention.
numbers: Performance peaks at intermediate planning frequency in Crafter and POGS (100 seeds). Planning every four steps beat planning at every opportunity.
limits: The mechanism is a hypothesis, supported by backtrack counts in POGS.
agent_relevance: Replanning every step can oscillate. Add a commitment rule: keep the plan until a surprise.

source: Ghoshal and Al-Bustami (2026) When Do Tools and Planning Help Large Language Models Think? A Cost- and Latency-Aware Benchmark
finding: Whether plan-execute-replan beats one-shot depends on the task. On Event-QA it helps (GPT-4o 47.5 to 67.5 percent) at huge latency. On persuasion (CMV) one-shot is best and planning adds cost without consistent gain.
numbers: 60 examples per task (3 splits of 20). Event-QA latency 8 s to 317 s per example for GPT-4o. CMV: GPT-4o-mini one-shot 75 percent at about 6 s (up to 85 percent on one split). Planning with search 25-35x slower for GPT-4o-mini.
limits: Small samples, two models, one LangGraph implementation. Multi-tool orchestration made the small model worse.
agent_relevance: A concrete case where a cached one-shot answer beats the planner, so the gate must be able to say 'no plan'. Cost in seconds is large against a 5 to 20 point gain.

source: Ghoshal and Al-Bustami (2026): failure modes and cost
finding: Small models degrade when planning needs many tools; the large model issued more search calls and longer traces. Authors advise caching tool results and planning only when structured evidence access is needed.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini costs 1/16.7 as much as GPT-4o. Event-QA best 67.5 percent at 317 s vs no planning 47.5 percent at 7 s (GPT-4o).
limits: Same small-sample limits as above.
agent_relevance: Plan only when the task needs evidence the cache cannot supply; cache tool outputs.

source: He and Feng (2026) When to Think Deeply: Inhibitory Deliberation for LLM Reasoning (IDPR)
finding: Response-conditioned arbitration. Take a fast answer, read its confidence, logit margin, parseability and cost, and call slow reasoning only when a learned controller expects gain. Framed on the expected value of control.
numbers: 5,000 held-out maths items: slow-call rate 8.20 percent, accuracy 47.90 to 48.92 percent (+1.02), average tokens 519 vs 5.26 fast-only. Random same-budget routing 46.76 percent; low log-prob 48.22; low logit gap 47.84. GSM8K 60.20 to 60.96; MoT 35.60 to 36.88.
limits: Gain is about one point and the fast model is weak (47.9 percent). The arbitration signal is the fast model's own confidence, like uncertainty arbitration in Daw 2005. Random routing hurts.
agent_relevance: A learned gate that sees the cheap answer beats random and simple thresholds, but by small margins. Expect modest gains from S0 gating alone.

source: He and Feng (2026) IDPR: corrective precision and utility
finding: The learned controller has the highest corrective precision, but cost-aware utility did not beat always-fast.
numbers: Corrective precision: IDPR 27.07 percent, random 13.41, low log-prob 21.22, low logit gap 11.46. Utility 0.4731 vs 0.4789 for always-fast.
limits: Under this token price the gate has no net payoff.
agent_relevance: Gate gains depend on token price. With cheap compute, always-fast can win on utility.

source: Zhang, Lin, Hou, Feng, Li (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: RL teaches a reasoning model to choose Thinking or NoThinking by difficulty. NoThinking is as good or better on easy problems; thinking only pays when problems are hard.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: average length -53.0 percent, accuracy +2.4. 7B: -40.1 percent, +2.3 (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME 2024). At lambda 0.05 the NoThinking share was 86.9 percent on GSM8K, 76.8 on MATH500, 40.4 on AIME. At lambda 0.1 length fell 64.5 percent but accuracy fell 0.5.
limits: Trained, maths only, distilled models. Accuracy gain shrinks as the NoThinking share rises.
agent_relevance: Cached (no-think) versus planned (think) choice per question, with a measured trade-off. Think share tracks difficulty.

source: Fang, Ma, Wang (2025) Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think
finding: Two control tokens (<short>, <think>) trained with DeGRPO cut long-chain thinking by 50 to 90 percent. A separate router LLM misjudges difficulty because it does not know the target model's own ability (AIME).
numbers: Base DeepSeek-R1-1.5B: reasoning models use 5 to 20x more tokens than concise ones. On GSM8K extended reasoning offers no clear advantage. Router Q-7B did not recognise AIME as hard even though the reasoning model reaches only 28 percent.
limits: Table rows are hard to align in extracted text, so per-row think-share was not verified. 1.5B model, maths. Vanilla GRPO collapses.
agent_relevance: The arbiter must know the executor's own competence, as in Daw 2005 where each system's own uncertainty drives control. Self-estimated competence beat an outside router.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: A Generative Agent with Fast and Slow Thinking for Complex Interactive Tasks
finding: An explicit fast module (imitation-learned small LM) plus slow module (GPT-4 plan and ground) with a rule-based switch. The most direct habit-versus-planner LLM agent.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types: SwiftSage 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3, SWIFT alone 49.2. Tokens per action: SwiftSage 757 vs SayCan 1,856, ReAct 1,971, Reflexion 2,983.
limits: Switch rules are hand written. Reflexion had up to four rounds, others one. Authors name a learned switch as future work.
agent_relevance: The four triggers are a usable S0 gate: escalate on stagnation (5 steps with zero reward), invalid action, critical decision, unexpected observation (a prediction error).

source: Liu, Wang, Wang, Guo, Li (2026) Imagine-then-Plan: Agent Learning from Adaptive Lookahead with World Models
finding: An LLM agent with a learned world model chooses its lookahead horizon (0 to Kmax) at each step. Learning when to imagine matters: removing the RL stage that trains the horizon choice drops success sharply.
numbers: Qwen3-8B without the RL stage: ALFWorld 88.57 to 71.42 percent, ScienceWorld 59.70 to 46.00 percent. Training-free ITP-I on Qwen2.5-7B ALFWorld 35.71 vs ReAct 27.86. Llama3.1-8B ScienceWorld test-seen 63.91 for ITP-R.
limits: Needs a world model; its quality is the main limit.
agent_relevance: Model-based control with variable depth is an explicit LLM-agent method, close to Sezener et al. 2019.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Imagine-then-Plan: adaptive versus fixed and random horizon
finding: Adaptive lookahead beat fixed-k and random lookahead at equal or lower cost. The gains come from choosing when to look ahead, not from looking further.
numbers: ALFWorld, 140 tasks in 14 folds, cost as normalised budget from total policy plus world-model tokens. Values are in plots and were not extracted.
limits: Exact figures not read.
agent_relevance: Depth should be chosen per state.

source: Da Pelo, Donvito, Frongia, Salis, Lieto (2026) Taming the Centaur(s) with LAPITHS
finding: Re-examination of Centaur (an LLM fine-tuned on human choices) on the two-step task. Standard LLMs given retrieval and only a task description come close to Centaur's choice fit, which weakens claims that fine-tuning installed human-like cognition.
numbers: Mean NLL per decision: Centaur 0.51, Llama 4 Maverick+RAG about 0.54, GPT-5.1 and GPT-4o about 0.55, Gemini 2.5 Pro about 0.56, DeepSeek R1 about 0.58, cognitive model 0.61, Llama 3.1 0.63. 150 trials, 300 decisions per model.
limits: Their NLL is sampling-based, Centaur's is token-probability based, so comparison is descriptive. Baseline SDs inferred from reported CIs. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Behavioural fit on two-step data does not show a model-based mechanism. Do not use two-step-like behaviour as evidence that an LLM plans.

source: Sun et al. (2026) NeuroCogMap Reveals Cognitive Organization of Large Language Models
finding: Uses LLM internals to propose a better dual-system model of human two-step data, with a dynamic arbitration weight, uncertainty-aware arbitration, omission and fatigue terms.
numbers: Held-out AIC, Two Step Task One: 262.45 vs original dual-system 268.77 vs behaviour-only discovery 268.73. Two Step Task Two: 465.95 vs 478.29 vs 473.53. Model form Q_hyb = w Q_MB + (1-w) Q_MF.
limits: Preprint; small AIC gains; the arbitration weight is fitted to human data, not shown to be an LLM mechanism.
agent_relevance: A mixing weight that changes over time fits humans better than a fixed one, so a scheduled planning weight is defensible.

source: Keramati, Dezfouli, Piray (2011) Speed/Accuracy Trade-Off between the Habitual and the Goal-Directed Processes
finding: Founding arbitration rule for the time-cost view: run the slow goal-directed system for an action only when the value of perfect information exceeds the cost of deliberation (average reward rate x deliberation time). Gives outcome-insensitivity after overtraining and sensitivity with equal-value choices.
numbers: Cost of deliberation = average reward rate x deliberation time. Simulated devaluation sensitivity early and loss after prolonged training (240 trials); kept when two equally valued actions compete.
limits: Simulation of rat data, not a human fit. Needs a Bayesian uncertainty estimate for each value, which an LLM does not natively have.
agent_relevance: This is the formula behind the S0 gate: plan when VPI exceeds reward rate x time. VPI could be estimated from disagreement among cheap samples.

source: Sezener, Dezfouli, Keramati (2019) Optimizing the depth and the direction of prospective planning using information values
finding: Extends the Keramati rule to tree search: expand a node when the value of information of the expansion beats the time cost; leaf values may be model-free estimates. Gives both depth and direction of search.
numbers: Speed/accuracy trade-off; punishment-induced pruning emerges from the rule. Proof-of-concept simulations.
limits: Simulations only; small trees.
agent_relevance: Template for best-first search with a stopping rule and a cached value at the frontier ('plan-until-habit').

source: Sezener et al. (2019): cost of the gate itself
finding: The rule needs only quantities already in working memory, so deciding what to expand costs little compared with expansion.
numbers: Text: choosing the best expansion has minimal memory cost; computational-time cost does not require computing the value for all strategies at each step.
limits: Theoretical argument.
agent_relevance: The gate must be cheap, otherwise it defeats its purpose.

source: Castro-Rodrigues et al. (2022) Explicit knowledge of task structure is a primary determinant of human model-based action (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: With minimal instruction, humans act model-free in a simplified two-step task. Model-based control appeared in only a minority and rose sharply once task structure was explained.
numbers: 204 participants: 109 healthy, 46 OCD, 49 other mood or anxiety disorders. Transitions 80/20. Instruction raised model-based control similarly in all groups.
limits: Simplified task, human clinical sample, not about LLMs.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, put the transition structure in the prompt. It is the cheapest route to model-based behaviour.

source: Model-Free RL or Action Sequences? (Frontiers in Psychology, 2019); authors not verified
finding: Competing explanation: chunked action sequences can mimic model-free reinforcement in two-step data. Two experiments dissociate them and find both operate.
numbers: Two experiments; sample sizes not extracted from the text I opened.
limits: Exact N and effect sizes not recorded. Check the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: Habit in an agent can be a cached plan (a macro) as well as cached values.

source: Feher da Silva and Hare (2020) Humans primarily use model-based inference in the two-stage task (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Failed-replication style result: with fuller instructions people look mostly model-based. Hybrid fits can label model-based agents with a wrong task model as hybrid. Seen via search summary only.
numbers: Three datasets per the abstract; numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; from search snippets.
agent_relevance: A 'model-free' reading of agent behaviour can be a wrong world model. Check the agent's model before blaming habit.

source: Binz et al. (2025) A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition (Centaur, Nature)
finding: Llama 3.1 70B fine-tuned on Psych-101 (over 60,000 participants, over 10,000,000 choices, 160 experiments) predicts held-out human choices; the two-step task is in the data. Seen via search summary only.
numbers: Two-step NLL 0.51 was read in the LAPITHS paper, not in the Nature paper.
limits: Not opened. Mechanism challenged by the LAPITHS preprint.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning on human choices can reproduce human mixes of habit and planning in behaviour, not necessarily the mechanism.

source: Akam, Costa, Dayan (2015) Simple plans or sophisticated habits? State, transition and learning interactions in the two-step task
finding: Model-free methods can reproduce a model-based stay-probability signature if they learn a latent state or use history, so the classic signature is not diagnostic. Known from a search snippet only.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. Do not quote numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Do not infer that an LLM plans from its stay-probability pattern alone.

source: Kool, Gershman, Cushman (2017) Cost-benefit arbitration between multiple reinforcement-learning systems (Psychological Science)
finding: People use more model-based control when it pays more in reward and less when it does not. Arbitration follows a cost-benefit comparison. From search snippets only.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports gating by measured pay-off, not by a fixed default.

source: Renaudo et al. (2015) criteria for shifting between goal-directed and habitual behaviours in robots
finding: Older robotics architecture with a meta-controller arbitrating between model-based and model-free modules by criteria. From a search listing only.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: An earlier machine example of an explicit arbiter with chosen criteria.
